name: Chiefdoms of the Ecuadorian Highlands (Cara, Panzaleo, Puruhá, Cañari, Palta)
summary: The peoples of Ecuador's Andean basins before and under Inca rule: the Pasto, Cara (Caranqui), Panzaleo, Puruhá, Cañari and Palta. They lived in competing chiefdoms, resisted the Inca for decades, and survive today as the Kichwa Sierra nationalities.

knownFor.label: Cañari gold work
knownFor.note: The Cañari were noted for fine gold working.

knownFor.label: Caranqui tolas
knownFor.note: Large earth mounds built by the Caranqui of the northern highlands.

knownFor.label: Pambamarca fortresses
knownFor.note: Inca forts built against the Cayambe chiefdom.

location.value: The Sierra, the Andean highlands of Ecuador, populated from north to south by the Pasto, Cara, Panzaleo, Puruhá, Cañari and Palta.
location.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era

terrain.value: Intermontane basins: the Caranqui, Puruhá and Cañari lived in the north, centre and south of the Ecuadorian Andes.
terrain.source: Bray, "Late Pre-Hispanic Chiefdoms of Highland Ecuador" (2008), abstract

migration.value: The Inca forcibly relocated many Cañari to other parts of the empire; the ancestors of the Saraguro are thought to be mitimaes (forced migrants) from Bolivia who married into local Cañari or Palta families.
migration.source: Encyclopedia.com: Cañari; eHRAF World Cultures: Saraguro Quichua

economicBase.value: The Sierra peoples were a sedentary, agricultural population; at Hacienda Zuleta in Imbabura, excavation found intensive raised-field agriculture (camellones) able to support dense populations.
economicBase.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era; Currie, Internet Archaeology 10

tradeRoutes.value: Lowland coastal peoples traded with the Sierra, exchanging fish for salt; Bray's chapter also covers long-distance exchange in all three regions.
tradeRoutes.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era; Bray, "Late Pre-Hispanic Chiefdoms of Highland Ecuador" (2008), abstract

governmentType.value: Independent chiefdoms (cacicazgos) in each basin, not one state; north of Quito they were competitive and often at war with each other. The older story of a Kingdom of Quito, supposedly ruled by the Cara, comes from a later chronicler and is not supported by ethnohistorical sources.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Pambamarca Fortress Complex; Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Caranqui political organization (abstract); Wikipedia: Cara people

institutions.value: Pre-Inca people lived in clans that formed larger tribes, and some allied in confederations; Caranqui mound sites (tolas) may have been religious rather than political centres.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian Ecuador; Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Caranqui political organization (abstract)

stability.value: The region was populated by distinct tribes that spoke mutually unintelligible languages and were often at war with one another.
stability.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era

majorWars.value: Inca conquest of Ecuador: one source dates its start to 1463 under the ninth Inca; another says Topa Inca Yupanqui may have begun it in the 1460s. The Cañari resisted strongly and were beaten by the 1470s; Huayna Capac then spent most of his reign on the north, where the Caranqui were finally beaten at Yawarkucha (Blood Lake), possibly as late as 1520.
majorWars.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era (1463); Encyclopedia.com: Cañari (Cañari beaten by the 1470s); Wikipedia: Pambamarca Fortress Complex (north completed possibly 1520; another popular source says 1500)

territoryChange.value: The Inca made the Cañari homeland a new imperial centre at Tomebamba and built a fortress complex at Pambamarca against the Cayambe chiefdom; Quechua replaced Cañari and Puruhá speech.
territoryChange.source: Encyclopedia.com: Cañari; Wikipedia: Pambamarca Fortress Complex

alliancesRivals.value: The Cañari backed Huascar against Atahualpa in the Inca civil war and were punished by Atahualpa's victory; they later assisted the Spanish conquerors.

inventions.value: The Cañari were noted for fine gold working.

religion.value: Caranqui mound complexes (c. 1250-1525) may have been religious centres, and Puruhá veneration of the volcano Chimborazo is the subject of a research paper; detail on beliefs is thin.
religion.source: Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Caranqui political organization (abstract); Cuadernos de Antropología (PUCE) contents

languageWriting.value: Several mutually unintelligible local languages; there is no recorded history from the Inca or pre-Inca cultures. After the Inca conquest Quechua replaced Cañari and Puruhá.
languageWriting.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era; Encyclopedia.com: Cañari

artsArchitecture.value: Gold working among the Cañari and monumental earth mounds (tolas) among the Caranqui, dated about 1250 to 1525.
artsArchitecture.source: Encyclopedia.com: Cañari; Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Caranqui political organization (abstract)

socialStructure.value: Clans grouped into tribes, with some confederations; the Puruhá are described in a student summary as a federation of lords with hereditary male succession.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian Ecuador; Universidad Nacional de Chimborazo course notes

sharedIdentity.value: Today these peoples are the Kichwa Sierra nationalities: Natabuela, Otavalo, Cayambi, Quitu, Panzaleo, Chibuleo, Salasaca, Waranka, Puruhá, Cañari and Saraguro.

neighbours.value: Pasto to the north in southern Colombia, coastal peoples to the west, and Amazon peoples to the east; the Inca Empire arrived from the south.
neighbours.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era

colonisation.value: Absorbed into the Inca Empire between the 1460s and about 1520, then conquered by the Spanish in the 1530s.

riseSignals.value: Chiefdoms formed in the basins: the Cara culture is dated from about 1000, the Puruhá culture 700-1450, and the Caranqui mound complex 1250-1525; these dates differ by source.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Cara people; Cuadernos de Antropología (PUCE) caption; Revista Española de Antropología Americana: Caranqui political organization (abstract)

outcome.value: Brought into the Inca Empire (Cañari in the 1470s, Caranqui possibly as late as 1520); the peoples survive today as the Kichwa Sierra nationalities.
outcome.source: Encyclopedia.com: Cañari; Wikipedia: Pambamarca Fortress Complex; Kichwa nationality document (CODEMPE list)

sources.value: Excerpts of Country Studies, Encyclopedia.com, Wikipedia (Pambamarca, Pre-Columbian Ecuador, Cara), Bray 2008 abstract, and a Caranqui abstract; read as search excerpts only, 17 Nov 2026. Spanish-language student notes (Universidad Nacional de Chimborazo) are weak and used only for the Puruhá succession note.

overallCertainty.value: No written record before the Inca; knowledge rests on archaeology and colonial chroniclers. Conquest dates differ by source (1463, 1460s, 1470s, 1500, 1520), and the Kingdom of Quito story is contested.
overallCertainty.source: Country Studies (US Library of Congress), Ecuador: Pre-Hispanic Era
